Before this Bill goes
out of committee, I should like to say a word on an entirely non-eontroversial subject. One of the abuses, if I may call it so, of the whole military system in Canada, and one which has brought most unmerited punishment upon the Administration, is the case of a man wdio attests at a different age from his real age. That has been a favourite trick. Men have said that they were of a certain .age, and since the Army Act does not provide that swearing to a false age is perjury, but provides the oppo-

site, they escape punishment. The consequence is that many of those men referred to by hon. gentlemen opposite, who landed in England performed various functions there and then returned or were rejected, got there solely because they said they were forty-four years of age when they were really fifty-four; and when they "were ready to return, they said that they were fifty-four, -and were returned accordingly. There are officers who are beyond military age and who know it. They were not rejected, and at any rate before 1917, they had in many oases good grounds for supposing that they could get to the front because the case of officers is somewhat different from that of men.
What is the age limit.for officers?

I am not aware that it is different from that for the men. In many eases it has happened that officers, well up, good men in good health, have got away to the front and have done nobly. Their eagerness has excused (their age. Other officers, whether non-combatants or otherwise, who have been most willing and determined to go to the front, did not get to the front because of being beyond military age. Other officers again, who did not want .to go to the front, did not get to the front, but remained in Canada, and those men are occupying preferential positions to which they are not entitled.
I am prepared to excuse, and I am sure all hon. members will excuse, the Administration in this regard, because no remedy is provided. I am bringing the subject up in ordeT that this House which, so far as I am aware, is theonly authority which can provide a remedy may provide one. This means more or less the adoption of an amendment to the Army Act which, as hon. members are aware, is adopted every year by Parliament in order to incorporate it in the law, since no longer is there a standing army in England or in the British Empire. The condition of affairs I have described has caused great and perennial scandal. Here are men and officers who know full well they will not be available, but they are occupying positions, whether as noncommissioned officers or as commissioned officers, drawing good fat pay which they could not get in other callings and blocking the way so that other men cannot rise to those positions. There are numerous cases of men who should be brought back from the front and put into those positions that are occupied by men in Canada who are not entitled to them, and who know full well they are not entitled to them. They 
may be high up, but they do not intend to go to the front. They will plead their age just as soon as it suits them and as soon as they require a stop-gap, but in the meantime they are floating about, and they are doing this country and this Government a great wrong. I have many times thought of bringing up this subject, and I hoped some one else would bring it up in the House; but since this military legislation is about to pass, I do not think it would be excusable longer to delay in bringing this matter to the attention of the House; nor do I think it would be excusable, after this legislation has passed, to bring it up again. Nothing is so much antagonizing the young men of the community and, indeed, the people generally, as seeing those men taking pet positions who have no intention of going to the front. I beg the Government to put a stop to this condition of affairs in the interest of recruiting and of the country.

I think the motion passed to reconsider section 6. 'That being the case, I am pleased to accept the amendment moved by the. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), I have worded it slightly differently, and perhaps it would be better if I made a motion amending the section. I, therefore, beg to move:
That the following be inserted as clause (5) of section 6, and that the present clauses (5) and (6) be numbered (6) and (7) respectively :-
(5) Each member of a local tribunal shall unless he be a judge make oath or affirmation that he will faithfully and impartially perform his duties as such member. Such oath or affirmation may be made before a judge, a justice of the peace, a commissioner for taking affidavits or before such other person as in any special case the minister may direct.
There is no change at all except in the last part of the sentence. It has occurred to me that there may be remote places where it would be a great inconvenience to compel the parties to travel to any of the officials named, and consequently, it was felt better that the minister m such case might direct some one else, such as the mayor or reeve of the town or village, to administer the oath. In this regard I may direct the attention of the committee to section 12 which provides that the Governor in Council may by regulation prescribe forms for the keeping of records. Consequently, it will doubtless be provided by regulation that a definite form will be sent to each tribunal, and also that a record of the oaths so made shall be kept. Amendment agreed to.

I desire to draw the attention of the House to section 16, as I propose offering certain amendments thereto for which I think there are very good reasons. This section provides penalties for interference with the work under the Act. Subsection. 3 says that any newspaper, book, periodical, pamphlet, or printed publication containing matter prohibited by subsection 2 may be summarily suppressed.
A newspaper, which is a business organization, and which involves a large investment of capital in many cases, is in a very different position from a book or pamphlet. The suppression of a book or pamphlet because of its containing objectionable matter merely destroys the investment made in the production of the bo6k or pamphlet, but the suppression of a newspaper or periodical amounts to the confiscation of the established business of that newspaper or periodical. I submit the conditions are so different between the newspaper and the book that they should not be placed in the same category as to suppression. While I do not think there is good or sufficient reason for the presence of this provision in the Act, still as the Government in its wisdom has decided to include it, I suggest as an amendment that instead of the business of the newspaper being summarily confiscated by suppression because it has been found to contain objectionable matter, the single issue of the newspaper or the periodical containing the objectionable matter might fairly be placed on the same level V book or. pamphlet, and the single issue of the newspaper or periodical might be suppressed summarily, as is provided in the section. The newspaper property should not be destroyed until after the owners have been given fair opportunity to argue their case and to bring whatever evidence they may see fit in support of their position, or in protection of their interests, just the same as any citizen is entitled to do in the protection of his personal liberty against the provisions of this section.
I move, seconded by Mr. Graham, that section No. 16 be reconsidered.
Motion agreed to.

I move, seconded by Mr. Graham:
That section 16 he amended by striking out subsection 3 and substituting the following: "Any issue, edition, or number of any newspaper, periodical, book, pamphlet or printed publication containing matter prohibited by subsection 2 of this section, may be summarily suppressed, and further printing or publication of the said matter in any future issue of any newspaper, periodical, book,
pamphlet, or printed publication, may be prohibited for any term not exceeding the duration of the present war, provided no action shall be taken under this subsection or under subsection 2 of this section without the approval of the Central Appeal Judge.
That replaces subsection 3 as it stands now, and provides only for the suppression of the single edition or issue of the paper or periodical. Then I would add, as subsection 4:
Any newspaper or periodical containing matter prohibited by subsection 2 of this section shall be deemed to be. a person within the meaning of said subsection 2, and shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable upon indictment before a Superior Court of the province in which the newspaper or periodical is published to be summarily suppressed by order of the presiding judge, and further printing and publication thereof may by such judge be prohibited for any term not exceeding the duration of the present war; provided that the editor, manager, or such other person as may be so designated by the owner or owners thereof shall be deemed by the judge to represent in person such newspaper ,or periodical in any proceedings that may be taken under this subsection.

I am sorry my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) did not give me notice of so important an amendment as this- an amendment involving consideration line by line. Subject to my inability to grasp the full effect of the amendment exactly, arising the moment he sits down, I would say that the amendment to clause 3 provides only for the suppression of the single issue which contains matter prescribed by the previous clause. I cannot see any value at all in the suppression of an issue of a newspaper after the contents of that newspaper have reached the Central Appeal Judge, because when the contents have reached the Central Appeal Judge and he has been able to come to a decision, the matter has reached everybody else in the country, and all the harm is done, and the newspaper would not care a fig whether you suppressed that issue or not. Under this amendment one might suppress until one was tired, and it would not do any good.
Then the amendment provides that the same matter which was objectionable in one issue must not be published in a future issue. I should not think it would be. Newspapers do not publish the same thing over and over again.
Sometimes they do.
May I suggest that this relates to the publication of the objectionable matter by any other newspaper.

But, that is forbidden anyway. What is the good of forbidding it

over again. Previous sections forbid the publication of the objectionable matter even by the first newspaper. Consequently, it is forbidden to the second newspaper or the third. It is repeating what the Act says before. It provides that thb same matter stiall not be published by any other newspaper or by the first offending newspaper. As far as it affects the other newspapers, such forbidden matter is already forbidden, and more language is merely surplusage. In so far a"s it affects the first offending newspaper, there would be no object in publishing the same thing over again. They would change the verbiage, but the effect would be the same, and they would pursue their course unmolested. As soon as their newspaper gets into the hands of their readers it is like snow in May, it is gone, the work is done, and suppression after the first offence is a purely futile punishment.
Now, as to clause 4; it says that once a newspaper commits this offence and publishes this objectionable matter, that newspaper is subject to prosecution just as a person is subject to prosecution under the previous section, and is liable to such punishment as befits a corporation or company. If the first clause were to remain, and if we were to adopt the futile methods which that clause prescribed, the second might be of some value rather than having nothing at all. But, inasmuch as in my judgment the first clause cannot remain, and we must retain the power of suppression or retain no effective power at all, then, of course, the fourth clause is of no value. So long as we have the power of suppression, there is no value in proceeding against the newspaper publishers as a company or as a newspaper. The power of suppression is quite sufficient. We have to retain that power of suppression or we have no power that is of any value for such a purpose at all. Let me draw attention to this fact: right up to this date, and ever since the war began, or since shortly after the war began, we as a Government have been empowered under the War Measures Act to take the proceedings which we ask to be authorized to take in this particular case. Under the War Measures Act, we have been authorized by Parliament to do that all along. Acting under the authority of the War Measures Act, we -have passed an Order in Council that enables a minister of the Crown, that enables the chief censor, on the authority of the Secretary of State and the Minister of Justice, to suppress a newspaper which contains matter in vio-
lation of that particular Order in Council. We have had that power all along, and we have had it unrestrained by any provision requiring us to obtain the approval of any central appeal judge or of a judge at all. Parliament felt at the opening of the war that that trial was necessary, and gave it to the Governor in Council. The Governor in Council passed an Order in Council enabling the Minister of Justice [DOT]and the Secretary of State to do this. Up to the present day no one has unjustly suffered and there has been no restraint. Unless we proceed by suppression we cannot proceed effectively because if we must proceed through the courts, a newspaper might conduct its objectionable campaign until the whole purpose of the Act, in so far as it was in its power, was defeated. Then, perhaps, we might get -a decision of the court. It is an ineffective remedy as applied to this particular violation of law. If we are going to. suppress this particular violation of law the remedy must fit the offence. It will, of course, be exercised most sparingly. Any power exercised under the Order in Council up to this date a regards these matters has been exercised very sparingly, every hon. gentleman will admit. The power will be exercised under the most definite restraint that a judge of the Supreme Court must first approve of its exercise, and I think Parliament may rely upon it, and it does rely upon it, that no iudge of the Supreme Court will harshly, hastily or without sufficient reason, suppress any newspaper in this country and thus bring great loss upon its owners. I think the protections, are sufficient. Experience has shown they are sufficient, and the essential features of the case show that the power is necessary.

People always feel more secure if they have m their defence a statute rather than the protection of even an honest and painstaking Government. If they have a law on the statute book which says they are protected by certain action that must be taken, they feel a little more secure even if taking of the action is altogether left to the discretion of the Government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is not left in this case

My hon. friend the Solicitor General points out that to suppress the issue of a newspaper would be no punishment, as the barm had been done. That is very true in a large measure, but the

same argument applies in a certain degree to the suppression of a book.
A book is a more permanent form of literature.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The difference
is very plain. The newspaper is read every day and the reading of a book may extend over months or years.

I said in a certain degree. The contents of the Tbook aTe not known until the book is circulated quite freely. The suppression of the book does not recall the harm that is done; it only provides against the harm being continued in the future. As far as the suppression of a book is concerned, m the first instance, no good accrues because the damage has been done, just as in the case of the newspaper in a measure. My hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) yesterday called attention to a certain book that had been suppressed. Every member of this House had a copy in his possession. As far as influencing members of Parliament is concerned, that seems to have been one of the objects, the harm had been done and the suppression of the book did not cure that harm. As far as the issue of this book was concerned, the suppression was no punishment at .all to the publishers. May I make the practical suggestion to the Solicitor General that in case a paper offends the issue offending be suppressed, and if the paper offends again between the time of the publication of its issue and the time of the trial before the judge, the censor would have the power of suppressing the paper altogether. That would be a medium course to take and the cause of the war would not have been prejudiced, because between the time of the publication of the first issue and the trial by the. judge, this paper would be precluded altogether from publishing, anything else of the same nature. I make that suggestion to the Solicitor General as a way out of the difficulty with full protection, I believe, to all parties. It is a little stringent to say that the goodwill in the entire business may be confiscated for the mistake of some individual on the staff, perhaps without the knowledge of the proprietor at all. It does seem a little harsh that the censor should have the arbitrary power t6 confiscate all the property.
Suppose that a farmer or any other citizen issued a .seditious circular or made a seditious speech, would he not think it harsh that the censor should have the right
not only to punish him for the speech but to confiscate his farm or other property as well? All the property the newspaper publisher has1-and the great majority have not full equity in that-is found in his newspaper plant, and under this Act he can be punished individually for what he says in his paper, and his entire property can be confiscated. Great offences require drastic remedies I admit, but in this case I think it is not unfair to say that suppression should not take place until the newspaper and the proprietor of that newspaper have had an opportunity to have a trial before a judge to see whether the matter complained of is seditious or not. The suggestion I make to the Solicitor General is, I think, not unreasonable, that the issue in which the seditious matter is found shall be suppressed and the newspaper restrained from publishing any seditious matter between the time of the first publication and the time of the trial before the judge. It strikes me that every interest would be protected if that could be done.

The suggestion of the hon. member is not at all open to the same objection as the former one. At the same time, it would hardly be an improvement. It really amounts to this, that the first offence goes unpunished, and only after a second can punishment be imposed. There is no such thing as suppressing an individual issue of a newspaper.
My hon. friend says it goes unpunished. But if it is proved before the trial judge that the article did properly come under the ban, the law takes its course.

That fuiure punishment remains under the Bill. But, in so far as effective action is concerned, it goes unpunished, because suppression is purely nominal as applied to a single issue. You simply cannot suppress a single issue. There would arise cases where it would be proper to warn a newspaper, and I do not think there has been one case where a newspaper has been proceeded against without previous warning. Often there have been repeated warnings, and that will undoubtedly continue to be the practice. It is quite conceivable that a case might arise of brazen, flagrant ' defiance of the whole Military Service Act, when the punishment provided in the Act should be properly applied. It would not be applied except in such cases. I do- not think it is fair to ask that the hands of the Government be tied in this regard, and that the

paper should be permitted to flagrantly, openly and defiantly declare its intention of violating this Act consistently, the -Government's only power being to say: Well, you have done it now, we invite you to do it once more. The amendment would leave the Government practically helpless in the face of such a situation.

My hon. friend forgets
his old friend " su'b judiee " in this matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, we have the judex there.

It makes a good deal of difference when'you are out shooting which end of the gun you are at, -and I have no doubt that .my hon. friend -the Solicitor General feels much more comfortable at his end of the gun than I do at mine; so he will perhaps excuse me if I express my sentiments from my point of view. As with many other newspaper men, everything we have in the world is in our newspaper and it is not the plant that is of serious value, it is the good-will that is of most material value. A newspaper is in one respect like a member of the animal kingdom-as soon as its circulation stops it dies. The stoppage of the publication of a paper amounts to confiscation of the property, and I cannot -see, as a newspaper man, any good reason why my property should be put any more in danger than that of any other man, or why the newspaper business should be considered .so exceptionally dangerous to constituted authority that rights which are elementary and universal as applied to every other -human activity and interest should be withdrawn from the newspaper. If it is true that there has been no exercise of that very great authority vested in the Secretary of State by the present stringent land drastic censorship regulations, and therefore the Government is entitled to credit for its careful exercise of this authority, may I suggest that on the other hand the newspapers, speaking of -them as a whole, have been just as careful to conduct their part of the public .service with due regard to the public interest in time of war. Except in one or two flagrant instances, I think -that it -must he accepted that the press of -Canada have accepted in good spirit and in good faith all the regulations and instructions issued by the censorship, although I anv bound to say, speaking as a member of the press, that for some of those regulations and instructions I could see no good and sufficient reason.
I think there is nothing in the history of Ithe press of Canada to give cause - for 
making it subject to a law which deprives it of the most elementary rights of citizenship, and treats it as though it were some objectionable institution which was dangerous to- .the welfare of the State. My hon. friend has made the suggestion that a newspaper which flagrantly defies the law should be suppressed. Surely there is nothing in the amendment I have offered to the House that would suggest the contrary. I am * admitting the right of the Government to -exercise its authority to suppress for well defined and established reasons, but I am protesting with all the strength I have against this position being assumed; that my property is absolutely subject to destruction by the Government without proof or evidence of offence on my part, and without the possibility of defence on my part. If this law is put into force my newspaper may be suppressed and my property confiscated although I have committed no offence against the law. I cannot admit that in this country of Canada there i-s -any condition or any probability of any condition that would warrant a law being placed on the statute-book that would put that power in the hands of a party Government to be exercised against their party opponents; that is the position.
I do not wish to go over the ground that I traversed on a former occasion here, but there is just one point I wish to emphasize. This Bill does not deal with offences against the State. It does not deal with treason, sedition, or giving information to the enemy. It deals and deals only with an offence against a law passed as a partisan measure by a partisan Government; and to give such a Government the power of destruction over their partisan opponents in the enforcement of such a law is to my mind by all means the greatest derogation from the liberties of the subject that has been perpetrated in this or any other country, so far as I know, up to the present time. I maintain again that there is nothing and has been nothing in the conduct of the press of Canada, as a whole, that warrants any such steps being taken.
As a matter of fact, this Bill was introduced into the House and received its second reading without containing these provisions depriving the subject of his liberty and of the right of free speech. It was only after the Bill had received its second reading that these provisions were inserted, and they were in such form and of such character that they were withdrawn and other provisions, certainly more under-

standable, inserted in their place, and it is with these provisions that I am dealing.
We are told that the Government may be trusted to exercise this terrible authority in the public interest alone. I took the liberty of bringing to the attention of the House yesterday an instance of the exercise of the authority vested in this Government under the War Measures Act, through the regulations regarding censorship. I showed that a pamphlet printed and published in England had been suppressed by order of the censor, and under the Order in Council and under the proclamation every man who holds a copy of that pamphlet renders himself liable to a fine of $5,000, or imprisonment, or both. What is the offence for which this pamphlet is placed under the ban? Is there treason within its covers? Is it an attack upon the welfare of the State? Sir, it is the most powerful arraignment of the liquor traffic of Great Britain that I believe has ever appeared in the English language or any other language in any country at any time, -and because that traffic has more friends than have the people of this country this pamphlet has been placed under the ban, and the authority of the censorship established, under the War Measures Act has been invoked for the purpose of preventing its circulation in this supposedly free' country of Canada. And it is this Government that asks the newspaper press of this country to accede to a law that deprives them of the right of defence when accused, deprives them of the right even of hearing the accusation against them, and miakes them subject to summary suppression at the hands of the Government.
I recall that it was my hon. friend the Solicitor General who brought in provisions to incarcerate a free citizen of this country in the tower of the Parliament buildings. I recall that it was my hon. friend the Solicitor General who introduced the closure into Parliament, .and I direct the attention of the country .to the fact that it is the Solicitor General who makes himself sponsor for this provision under which he and his colleagues during the election that is about to take place can hold out the threat of suppression against every newspaper in Canada, and make the threat good. I recall that in Manitoba in the year 1912, under the administration of the law as it prevailed in that province, men were thrown into jail without a charge, and, after being held there through the election, were released without trial. I recall that when that question was raised in this
House, every man on the other side, from the Prime Minister down, voted in justification of that action.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What action is my hon. friend talking about?
I am speaking about the maladministration of justice during the Macdonald election in Manitoba in the year 1912.
May I ask the name of the man who was put in jail?
Wagner.
Sullivan, was it not?

I do not recall the name. Perhaps it was Sullivan; I do not remember. I do know, however, that three men were put in jail under those circumstances, and my hon. friend stood up in his place and justified by his vote that maladministration of justice; that deprivation of the liberty of the subject. On the eve of a general election, I shall be excused if I recall these events and assert that this provision was put in this Bill, after the second reading, with a view to the forthcoming general election and for the purpose of gagging the press of this country.

Perhaps I should
apologize to the committee for daring, after so long a series of crimes against the liberty of the people, to rise to speak before a free Parliament. I am depicted by the member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) as author of the incarceration of one Miller, who, against the law of the land, refused to answer questions respecting his conduct as a beneficiary of the moneys of this country and took the punishment which the law of the land entailed. I am not the author of the provisions under which he received that punishment. They are older than myself, older than the hon. member for Edmonton, as old as the British constitution. I trust that they will be in full force and buoyancy when both of us shall have passed from the earth.
That is a good Tory wish.

I had something to do with, though I did not introduce, the closure resolution to which the hon. member refers. I took some small part in the debate, and my memory is green enough \o enable me to recall some of the incidents that took place during that debate. I remember that the member for Edmonton was, perhaps, the loudest among many in

proclaiming to what he thought was an outraged country that Parliament was to he throttled; that free discussion was to he murdered; that he spoke then for the last time in a free Canadian Parliament. He could not have brought to the committee a better illustration to make plain to every one the folly of hiis own predictions now. Let him reflect for a moment on the prognostications that he made four years ago when the closure resolution was introduced. Free discussion was to be a thing of the past. Parliament was to be gagged just as he says now the press is to be gagged. Hon. members could no longer feel the freedom that they had felt before; he looked forward to a time when he would not be allowed to stand in this House and discuss the subjects of the day as- he had done in days gone by. The member for Edmonton himself is the very best of many illustrations of the folly and the failure of his own prognostications.
In this legislation we are not departing from any British principle that I ever heard tell of. It is not departing from British principle to say that if a man disobeys the law he shall then and there
9 p.m. be forbidden to disobey again, and if necessary prevented by physical' restraint from disobeying. That is the law of the land, imbedded in almost every criminal statute. If a man runs amuck and commits murder he is not told to go ahead and commit murder until the first offence is brought before a tribunal and he is tried for it. No; he is taken in hand by the physical arm of the law and he is put behind bars, where he can no more commit what he has committed. There he awaits his trial, 'long before he is proved guilty. The same holds true of every offence that a man may commit.
But he is not punished until he is tried.
Yes, he is punished before he is tried, by the punishment of restraint.
But you propose to take authority to suppress a newspaper, without notice and without trial.

I have very great respect for the judges of the Supreme Court, but a judge of the Supreme Court does not give judgment against me on the most trivial offence or in the most trivial case without my having an opportunity of stating my case or of having it stated for me before him; but under this measure a judge of the Supreme Court will render his decision on a statute made by the Government or its friends without my having any opportunity of stating my case.
Why does the hon. member say that?
Where does the Bill say that a judge of the Supreme Court will give me such an opportunity?
He certainly will in any first case.

There is no provision whatever for his doing so. It is .not contemplated in the Bill that there shall he any such notice or any such opportunity, and every argument that my hon. friend has made here within the last hour indicates that there is no such intention. This, he says, has tct be an exercise of authority on the instant, or there can be no sufficient protection of the public interest. I maintain that there is no such condition as requires my being deprived of the meet elementary right of a citizen in dealing with a judge of the Supreme Court.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If my hon.
friend were a judge of the Supreme Court, would he render a decision without giving the newspaper proprietor an opportunity of stating his case?
I would not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Then why does
he imagine that any judge of the Supreme Court'would do so? '

Because a judge of the
Supreme Court is given a statute-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
So would my
hon. friend.

But a judge of the Supreme Court is given a set statute in which there is no provision for, nor any suggestion of, any right of representation by the newspaper, and therefore he would be in duty bound to act upon the recommendation made to him by the Secretary of State or by the Government or by its agents. There is no provision in the Bill for calling in The newspaper proprietor to make a defence. It would be absurd to suppose that a judge of the Supreme Court would go so far outside of the provisions and the evident intent of the statute, no matter how just he might think it would be to do so. My hon. friend made much of the fact that criminals were not allowed to run at large; that when an offence was committed the criminal was at once seized and prevented from committing the same offence again. My hon. friend's suggestion in regard to the administration of the law reminds me of the Englishman who w>as frequently called on a jury, and he was asked how, in his large experience, he made up his mind as to the verdict he would give. "Well," he said, "I looks him over, and I says to myself: If he did not do it, why is he there?" So my hon. friend places before the House the suggestion that the procedure with criminals is to punish, them whether there is a trial or not.
I should think that in the profession he follows, he would recall that there are such things as trials; that there is such a thing as a prisoner being allowed oult on bail; that there is such a thing as a jury of twelve men standing between the law and the criminal before the law can be enforced; and that the incarceration of a suspected man in jail is not the same as the suspension of a newspaper. The parallel case would be, just as my hon. friend sketched it to the House-that the prisoner was executed, and then a trial was held. He proposes that the newspaper shall be destroyed, and then-well, that is all there is to it. The newspaper will then he out of the Government's way.
Carried.

Not for a few minutes. I will not detain the committee long. There is a vital objection to this section in that it provides that summary action will be taken and a newspaper may be suppressed without any notice to the proprietor. It is not enough for the minister to say

that any judge having common sense would give notice. There is no provision fox notice being given. There is nothing in the section which would indicate to the judge for a single .moment that it was the intention of Parliament that notice should be given. If this section passes in its' present form, it indicates the clear intention of Parliament that the proceedings should be ex parte, and that the judge ishould act in an ex parte manner without the proprietor of the newspaper having any opportunity of being heard. That is contrary to the most elementary principles of justice; it is allied with what this Government have asked Parliament to do when they have taken awiay the sacred right of habeas corpus, a right which was wrested from the authorities by the British people over three hundred years ago and which has existed in every British country since then. If the ministers had given any thought to this question, they would have provided that before this summary action should be taken the proprietor of the newspaper man should have notice, should be summoned before the judge, and should be given an opportunity of stating his objection to the action being taken. It might be that lie could show that the article complained of did not bear the meaning attributed to it by the authorities. He might be able to show that the article complained of was published without his authority, without his knowing anything about it, or during his absence. Surely this law ought to provide that he should have an opportunity of stating his defence to the proposed action, but this section provided that his newspaper may be destroyed. That is the effect, because we all know that when you have destroyed even the one issue of a newspaper, you inflict upon the proprietor an irrevocable, damage. What would be the objection to provide in this section, just as is proposed by the amendment, that notice should be given to ithe proprietor of a newspaper before action is taken? This section provides that, simply on the approval of the Central Appeal Judge being obtained, the newspaper may be suppressed; and an order may be made preventing its republication at any time during the period of the war.
My hon. friend the Solicitor General says if a man commits a crime he is not left at large, but is arrested. That is perfectly true, but the law provides that he cannot be kept in prison without a [ireliminary examination which must take place almost immediately, and which must be held in 
a public court, when he will have an opportunity of bedng represented by counsel and of cross-examining the witnesses who may be called by the prosecution. That is an opportunity which the law has provided for the benefit of every man, no matter how vile a criminal he may be. If there is a long or unreasonable delay in bringing him before the (magistrate for preliminary examination, he has that sacred right under the Habeas Corpus Act, and he can apply to the judge who will issue an order to the jailer compelling him to show cause why that man is held in custody. In this case no such right is accorded to the proprietor of the newspaper. Proceedings may be taken against him summarily, and his whole property may be destroyed without notice. This is a provision entirely contrary to every principle of justice, and it is an unnecessary provision, because no great harm can be done by delaying for two or three days, or even a week, before final action is taken, thereby giving the man who is charged the same opportunity as is afforded to a criminal no matter how low nr how vile he may be, the opportunity of making his defence before final action is taken against him. It seems to me that the Solicitor General would be well advised if he would so frame this section as to have some regard for the principles of justice which prevail at this day in connection with the ordinary administration of law so far as any criminal is concerned. It is truly said that those whom the gods wish to destroy they first make mad. I think they have made this Government mad, when they have come to Parliament and taken away the most sacred right and the most sacred privilege that a British subject enjoys today, the right of appearing before a judge to determine why he is being held in jail. They have taken away that right, when they have provided that one of the greatest safeguards of liberty in this country-the press-may be summarily silenced and summarily put out of existence without any opportunity of being heard.
Amendment (Mr. Oliver) lost on division.

Might I ask the Solicitor General a question? Possibly the matter has alreadv been explained, but I would like to be informed regarding it. The marginal note to subsection 5 of section 11 says: "Penalty for applying to more than one local tribunal for certificate." In what cases is it apprehended that more than one application will be made for a certificate?

We give every man the privilege of choosing his own tribunal in his own province. The object of this subsection is to prevent a man passing from one tribunal to another-say, having his application rejected by one and then trying another.
From one province to another?
No. From one tribunal to another in his own province. Once a man selects his tribunal he has to abide by bis selection.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall I report the Bill.

I think the Solicitor General should at least outline in Hansard the rules of procedure by which a man will come before a judge for the suppression of a newspaper or for taking any action. I think the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) is quite right in saying there should be some procedure provided. We know ex-parte motions are made every day, and I think there should be some procedure by which a notice will be given to the other side, giving them an opportunity to come before the judge and show cause why they should not be punished. We are in the dark as to what line of procedure should be followed.

I do not think there is any particular procedure about it. If it were to be taken as a matter of legal procedure and formality there would be no practical way of preventing the continued publication of objectionable and illegal matter, particularly in distant newspapers. For example, a newspaper in Vancouver would have to lay its case before the judge in Ottawa, and by the time they did that a very great deal of harm might be done in Vancouver. I apologize to Vancouver for even suggesting that any such literature might appear in that city; I only mention it by way of suggestion.
As an illustration, there is an Order in Council dated, I think, November 5, 1914, which proscribes a certain class of literature from publication and circulation in Canada. That Order in Council provides that the Secretary of State may, if such literature is published in a newspaper, take possession of the newspaper plant, prevent publication, place a censor in the plant if he desires, or compel the editor or proprietor of the paper to submit all articles to a censor before such articles are published. As a precautionary step this Order in Council provides that before the Secre-.
tary of State takes that action he shall first secure the approval of the Minister of Justice. The procedure is simply this: The Secretary of State has a case under consideration. He lays the facts before the Minister of Justice by way of memorial, and if the Minister of Justice approves of the intention of the Secretary of State as expressed in the memorial, he simply writes across it that he so approves. I presume much the same procedure would be followed here, that the facts of the case- and the facts would consist of the article itself-

If my hon. friend will pardon me. The Prime Minister said, in answer to the hon. member for Edmonton: " Does the hon. member suppose that any judge would grant such an order without hearing the other side?" That implies there shall be a hearing. How is that hearing to >be brought about?

I presume the facts of the case would be laid before the Central Appeal Judge by way of memorial, and the facts would consist, in my judgment, of nothing more or less than the article itself. All the Central Appeal Judge would have to do would be to compare the article with the law, and I do not see how an argument would have very much place, although it might have some.
He would compare the article with the law and he would be guided by his common sense and a regard for the interests of the state as to whether or not the violation was such as to call for a summary remedy. Where there was no open defiance or flagrant challenge of the power of the law, or where there was perhaps some doubt as to the real intention of the writer, the judge might consider it a case in which the writer should be heard, and possibly warned. All he would have to do would be to telegraph the writer or the newspaper publishers and state that up to a certain time he would be willing to hear them as regards this offence. That is all the procedure that would be necessary. Or, he might communicate with them in some other way. It would be very ill-advised if we were to set about legislating any particular machinery into the operation of this Act in this regard by the Central Appeal Judge.
Has the Government considered the advisability of placing the censorship under the Department of Justice rather than under the Secretary of State as it now is?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The Minister of Justice has control of effective action in the way the Solicitor General has already mentioned, for dealing in a summary way with a newspaper. The Secretary of State, under the terms of the Order in Council, must submit to the Minister of Justice the considerations upon which the proposed action is based, and the Minister of Justice must approve. The censorship is dealt with almost altogether by the officers appointed for thaii purpose, and we have little to do with it. These officers come to us for direction whenever it is necessary. I do not remember that on more than half a dozen occasions during the last three years has the subject been brought to my attention. But in order that there might be definite safeguards, we did, a year or nine months ago, appoint a committee of the Privy Council. The Solicitor General is convener of that committee. Whenever any matter of importance, upon which the direction of the Government is desired by the censors, is brought up for consideration, it goes to that committee of which the Minister of Justice, the Solicitor General and the Secretary of State are members. I think there are one or two other members of the Government who are on that committee, but I cannot recollect who they are. These matters are really dealt with altogether in that way. I would not like my hon. friend from North Gape Breton (Mr. McKenzie), or my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), to understand, or to regard it as essential in every Case, that notice should be given. There might be a case so absolutely glaring, so malicious, so dangerous, that the Central Appeal Judge would consider that he should not even wait for a copy of the paper but would be willing to deal with it upon a telegraphic. report of a deputy censor or other reliable authority. But in ordinary cases matters are not dealt with in that way. The newspaper has been warned two or three times, perhaps, or even oftener, that its course is not in accordance with the regulations laid down. We all know, of course, that a newspaper may introduce matter in its columns when those who are responsible for its management know nothing about it. It might be done altogether inadvertently and, in so far as that newspaper is concerned, it would be most harsh and unjustifiable to deal with a case of that kind without some injury as to the way in which such a thing had happened. No such practice has ever prevailed, and I am quite confident that it 
never would prevail-certainly, it would never prevail with my consent or approval. The whole question is more or less surrounded with difficulties and perhaps there were in the earlier part of this war more difficulties in this country than in most countries, more difficulties obviously than in Great Britain. There were many matters which it would be very inadvisable in the public interest to have published, and yet for nearly 4,000 miles our boundary ran along that of -the great neighbouring nation which was neutral in the war and in which, of course, no censorship regulations prevailed. The difficulty was to create such conditions in Canada as would prevent the publication of undesirable information in the United States. There was a good deal of difficulty about that. We had to take rather extreme powers under the War Measures Act for the purpose of preventing it. I think I am justified in saying to the committee that the censorship regulations have been so effective, and the press of the country and all the news agencies have worked so loyally in co-operation with the Government, that I myself am told of important incidents that have happened in this country and were never published, were never known even to the members of the Government generally, and which it was extremely important should not be known by the public. I could, if it were desirable, give to the committee a great many illustrations of that, and I have been very much impressed from time to time, when matters of this kind were brought to my attention, with the splendid, effective way in which the press and the news agencies of the country have, with occasional trifling exceptions, co-operated with the Government and the censorship authorities in bringing about such a condition.	,

It is well worth while to have the views of the Prime Minister and the Solicitor General upon this matter. It is not a light thing to put such a drastic power in operation without giving the object of it at least an opportunity of defending himself. I am sure the Solicitor General and the Prime Minister are quite familiar with the practice in this matter in our courts. What is proposed to be done here, if it is done at all, is nothing more or less than the parallel of a perpetual injunction proceeding. No perpetual injunction is granted without first, if necessary, an interim injunction for the purpose of giving an opportunity of going into the case and seeing whether the interim injunction

should or should not be made perpetual. If there was any urgent call an interim order could issue stopping the publication in the meantime and an opportunity could be given at a later date to make the interim injunction perpetual if necessary. Why should it be made perpetual in the first instance? That is what we are protesting against.

I wish to welcome my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) back from his trip to Washington. During his absence I called the attention of the right hon. leader of the House to a vexed question which has some relation to this Bill; indeed it arises out of the enactment of the conscription law. Several young men who under this legislation are liable to be called out have written me stating that they carry life insurance, and that if they are forcibly enlisted the insurance companies will immediately raise their premiums to the standard of their war risks. Has the minister decided to implement the present legislation with a view to either paying that premium out of Government funds or fixing by amendment to the Insurance Act a maximum premium? I understand, in fact I know, that the insurance companies would not relish the idea of carrying insurance on the lives of soldiers at their normal rates of premiums, but, on the other hand, I would ask the minister if it is fair in such a case as this that a young man who carries insurance should be compelled by the effect of this legislation to pay perhaps double the premium on his life insurance. It seems unfair that a young man should lose all the benefits of all his past payments upon an insurance policy or that he shall have to incur heavy liabilities for the payment of his premiums in future. It may be that a young man will find some friend or relative who will make the payments in his absence and agree to ' pay the extra premium, but that must be the exception. What does the Government intend to do under those circumstances? We are told that it is the will of the country that 100,000 men should be secured to reinforce our boys at the front. We are told that this legislation, while drastic in its nature, is absolutely necessary. We are told, indeed we know, that as a result of this legislation young men will have to don the khaki and go into the trenches and possibly never return. I quite realize this condition of things, 'but at the same time, as was well proven in the course of
228i
this debate and notably on the occasion of the amendment moved the other day by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), it is established beyond perad-venture that there are men in this country making huge profits, and those profits are made because of the war conditions. Not later than last week a report was published on the authority of the Government . in which it was established that certain cold storage companies were piling up huge, scandalous profits. Will not my hon. friend take heed of what public opinion is demanding at the present time, and if it is necessary to recruit or to enlist under this law * 100,000 young -men, and if as a result of that enlistment the savings of those yeung men as represented by their insurance policies are lost or threatened, will he not see to it that the war profiteers Shall pay enough out of their profits to make up the difference between the ordinary premium and the war premium which is being asked by the insurance companies? I am in earnest in making this plea. The United States, on the occasion of the conscription legislation passed by the United States Congress, adopted a measure which meets the condition I have already described. The Prime Minister yesterday gave us to understand that this question had received the earnest and serious consideration of the Minister of Finance. This Bill is now practically passed. It will in a few moments he reported to the House to be taken into consideration for its third reading on Tuesday next, I understand: Perhaps my hon. friend is not in a position this evening to giye out to the country the decision which has been arrived at on this question of premiums. If he is not ready to .make a full statement just now, I would ask him to do so before the third reading, after he has taken into consideration the facts which I have	to his attention.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The matter drawn to the attention of the committee by the hon. member is one of great importance and also of great difficulty. It is not possible for me to make a definite announcement upon this subject, which I have had more or less under consideration for some time past. At my request the Superintendent of Insurance has been looking into the whole matter of the insurance of Soldiers, with a view to ascertaining the nature of the insurance contracts covering soldiers' lives, and the increased financial responsibility which would devolve upon the companies by reason

-of the additional risk of carrying the policies of soldiers at the front.
I	gather from what my hon. friend has said that it was made clear to the House yesterday that there would be very considerable additional financial responsibility upon insurance companies. The rates of insurance companies have regard to the risk, and if the risk is greatly increased the companies, subject, of course to the terms of their policies, would naturally desire to increase the premium or terminate the policy. This is not a new question. It came up in connection with the voluntary enlistment system, and 1 do not think the question to-day is any different from the question that arose in connection with the insurance of those who volunteered their services.
The Canadian Patriotic Fund has been keeping on foot the policies of hundreds of soldiers who have gone to the front, for the benefit of their families. It must not be overlooked that the Government is providing pensions for the families of soldiers who fall in this war, and that fact must be taken into consideration when ithe question of insurance is being considered. When in civil life a citizen insures his life for the benefit of his family; if he dies the insurance policy is a very valuable asset to his estate, but there is no pension from the estate. When a citizen enlists, however, and goes to the front and falls in battle, there is a pension for his family and that is a consideration which we must bear in mind.
It would not seem to me off-hand that the insurance companies should be compelled to assume a greatly increased risk without some consideration from the Government. I cannot speak off-hand as to the terms of the policies. In some policies, I presume, there is a voidance clause in the event of war and the insured enlisting and being killed in battle.
My hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) has mixed up with this question of insurance-and to that extent weakened what was otherwise a strong argument-some references to profiteers and the duty of the Government to provide money in connection with this insurance by taking away the profits of those who have made money during the war. I would like to say this to my hon. friend: The Government has not been neglectful of its duty with regard to the taxation of profits made by those engaged in business in this country. I say further, and this cannot be controverted, there is no war tax in the world to-day in any country that is now at war that is heavier than the Business Profits War Tax brought in under the Bud-
II	Sir Thomas White.]
get of this year. I say that with the most absolute confidence; it cannot be contradicted. The United States is considering a taxation measure at the present time which does not begin to approach the Business Profits War Tax of the Dominion of Canada.

What about the income
tax in the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is a different matter. The income tax is a small tax as compared with the Business Profits War Tax. It may be two, or three or four per cent, but in Canada we are taking, as my hon. friend knows or ought to know, one-quarter of the profits from seven to fifteen per cent, one-half of the profits from fifteen to twenty per cent, and seventy-five per cent of the profits over twenty per cent. That is a very heavy tax indeed. It is the heaviest taxation in the world to-day upon war profits, and that fact cannot be over-emphasized because it has been misrepresented to the country. When I introduced the Business Profits War Tax I was severely attacked by hon. gentlemen opposite on the ground that it was too severe a tax-not because it was not severe enough. Let us be perfectly fair and frank about this mattej:. I laid it down in the Budget that those who make profits out of this war should contribute most to the expenses of the war, and that policy we have carried out.
My hon. friend, I think, impaired his argument with respect to insurance by dragging in this irrelevant question of undue profits, of which we have heard so much in this House. What I object to is that when I bring in a measure, as I did in the Budget, for the" taxation of business profits in this country, hon. gentlemen opposite object that the tax is too severe, and then afterwards accuse me of being too considerate with respect to the profits made in this war.	'
Coming back to the question which I assume my hon. friend has most at heart, namely, the -insurance of soldiers, I am not able to make a definite statement to-night, nor do I think it necessary that this Bill should be delayed until a definite statement is made. The situation is not materially different from the situation that existed with reference to those who went forward under the voluntary system; they also had insurance. As I stated, this whole matter is under consideration by the Superintendent of Insurance, and after I get his report and know precisely what are the various elements involved, I shall be in a position to deal with the matter.
If the Finance Minister will do me the honour of reading the few remarks I made on this subject when the hon. member for Rouville 'brought it up yesterday, it will save my repeating them now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall be very glad to.

I have been requested to ask the Prime Minister this question: Is he sure that the wording of the clause referring to exemptions, where the word " minister " is used, would include the officers of the Salvation Army, for example? They are not called ministers; they have the designations of officers in the army- captain, lieutenant, and so on. Is my hon. friend sure that they will be included in the exemptions under the clause as it is now worded?

I support my hon.
friend's contention that the officers of the Salvation Army ought to be exempt.
Mr. ME1GHEN: Any one who as a matter of practice officiated in the Salvation Army as a minister officiates in relation to his congregation would come under the terms of this provision, because the Salvation Army is a religious denomination. Any one in the Salvation Army who acted the part of minister, even though he might not be known as such, would be entitled to the same exemption as any one acting in a corresponding capacity in another denomination.
Question.

Let us take time to'consider this matter; if it should happen that some very influential body suffered an injustice, every member of this committee would be sorry that he hurried. If the Government is sure on this point, I have nothing more to say. Could not the language be changed so that it would include any person in any denomination acting in a capacity corresponding with that of minister in a regularly constituted denomination? For instance, in one organization those who officiate are called readers; the word "minister" is not used.

I do not think there is any doubt at all that the effect of the exception is to include such persons. A man does not need to be known as a minister to come under its provisions. I am not very familiar with the terms used in all denominations, but I think that in the Anglican Church the person known as minister in some other denominations is known by another name. No one would suggest for a moment that persons acting in that capacity were not exempt.
Perhaps they would be included under the term "clergy."

They may be included in the definition of clergy; undoubtedly they would also be included in the term "ministers of all religious denominations." Consequently, any one acting in a similar capacity in the Salvation Army is clearly included. I recognize that this matter is one of great importance; that 10 p.m. it would be the greatest injustice if the Salvation Army should be treated differently from other denominations. However, in my judgment the Act clearly covers that denomination.
Perhaps it is not a denomination, legally speaking.
I think they disaffirm the idea that they are a denomination.

I believe that they are incorporated; those who officiate amongst them have power to marry, as other ministers have. Could instructions be given to the tribunals that the word "minister" includes all such persons?
That could be done by regulation under the clause which provides for uniformity. It would only be a matter of uniform application.
If you are to draw regulations-
Carried.
No, not carried.

Bill reported, amendments read the first and second time and concurred in, on division.

speechtext: To-morrow and Saturday are rather inconvenient days upon which to take up the third reading if there should be debate or division. The House in Committee on Bill No. 13, to consolidate .and amend the Railway Act. -Hon. Frank Cochrane. (Resumed from Wednesday, July 16).
Mr. D. Stewart in the Chair.
On section 393-Disobeying orders of board.

Subsection 2
renders the officers of the company-the president, vice-presidents and managers- liable to very heavy damages for disobeying the orders of the board. Subsection 3 provides a penalty for municipal officers who do not obey the orders of the board, and subsection 5 shows that the board has full charge of all prosecutions in connection with the matters involved.
This section, I presume, would apply to a railway company that declined to give the required information lor .a statistical report?
Undoubtedly.

I suppose the minister has had the experience that others have had before him of the difficulty of securing such information from some of the railway companies. This section applies to that disobedience to the orders of the board?
Yes.
Not only does it apply to any railroad corporation, but it applies to any corporation or municipality over which the board has any control.
Has the board any control over municipalities?
The section says very distinctly-

It says so, but has it any right to say so?
[Bir Robert Borden.]

Subsection 3
says:
Wherever it is proved that any municipal or other corporation has neglected or refused to obey any order of the Board made under the provisions of this Act, the mayor, warden, reeve or other head of such corporation, and every member of the council or other ruling or executive body of such corporation, shall each be guilty of an offence for which he shall be liable to a penalty of not less than $20 and not more than $5,000.
We have taken a chance for several years trying to control municipalities that are under provincial control; I suppose we shall keep on doing - so until we are stopped?
What procedure is provided for the enforcement of the penalty?

Nothing more than the procedure provided for in subsection 3 which I have just read. In addition to that, the section compels the president, the	vice-president-each	vice-president,
where there are more than one-and every director and managing director-
I am not asking the hon. member about that; I quite understand that; but I presume there is a method of enforcing those penalties provided somewhere in the Act?
Yes.

Penalties may be enforced summarily in an ordinary court; or they may be enforced by indictment. How are those penalties enforced?
Mr. J, E. ARMSTRONG: The board have the machinery to carry out the provisions of this section.

The penalties will not be inflicted by the board. The cases would have to go to the courts of the country to have the penalties imposed.-Section agreed to.
On section 395-Purchase of railway securities.

The committee amended the first subsection. After the word "Act" in the eighth line, the words "or the Special Act" are inserted. The committee will understand that this Act refers to the Special Act in many cases, and in this one in particular where the words have been added.

Section agreed to.
On section 399-Removing industrial spurs without leave.

This section has been recast and made negative as well as

positive. The effect will probably be to increase the powers of the board, but it is conceded it is difficult to know what the meaning of the former section 365 was.

This section provides a penalty for removing a spur or branch line constructed under or pursuant to this Act. An industrial spur is always put in at the expense of the company or person who wishes it. The railway company furnishes the rails on the ordinary standard agreement by which the company or person pay? the cost of the labour and the ties. The local parties pay interest or rental on this spur. The spur becomes the property of the company or person using it. If they have paid for it and it is their own property, why should they be liable to a penalty if they remove it?
I understand the penalty is on the railway.

The section reads:
Any company or person who, without consent or order of the Board, removes any spur-[DOT]
I am not objecting to the section, but I never could understand it. There may be a previous section which provides that the board has the right to allow a second corporation or person under such terms as it thinks proper, the right to use a spur that is being put down for another person. I know of a case-and I am not going to say anything that will cause the minister .any unpleasant thoughts-where the Intercolonial took up a .spur without any trouble at all.
I received a very large petition for the removal of that spur.

I have not heard that
the Intercolonial have paid any penalty for removing that spur. If the Intercolonial came under the authority of the Eailway Board, if they remove a spur again, they will be liable to a penalty.
Mr. COpHRANE: There was no authority for putting down that spur, and it inconvenienced many people. I have in my office a large petition for the removal of that spur.

I am not going to argue that. I have seen the petition, and I have travelled over every part of the locality in which the spur was. Nobody was inconvenienced, and there was no earthly reason why that .spur was taken up except political reasons. A young man started in to do business in competition with three men who, for fifteen years, had carried on all
the business in that community. He paid his money and got his spur put in, and he was shipping potatoes and doing a nice business. In three weeks his spur was taken up. There was a street leading down to the wharf, and there was also a private way leading to .the wharf, and there were three or four houses on this private way.
You cross over the street and go up to the railway station without crossing the track at all, or, if you came up the private way you simply had to cross this spur. I just want to tell the minister, there is no amount of objection no amount of sophistry, and no argument or anything that can be said, which for one moment would justify the taking up of that spur. However, it was done by the Intercolonial and not by a private company, so I suppose there is no use discussing .it.

Section agreed to.
On section 404-Improper use of highways.
The only change .made in this section is in the last line. The words " nor more than $5,000 " have been added.
That limits the damages.

That is the
penalty for improper use of the highways.

I was wondering whether it' was .advisable to include that amendment. The law as it stood provided that the railway company should be liable to a penalty of not less than $40, and there was no maximum. It is now provided the maximum shall be $5,000. I can quite understand there might be circumstances under which a railway company would be willing to pay $5,000, and even more than $5,000, to get the right to use a street.
Would that give them the right?

I will give my hon.
friend an illustration. About twenty years ago, in the town in which I lived there was a tmill-owner who wanted to get a .spur track from the railway siding into his mill. In order to do this he had to go about forty rods, along the main street of the town. The town authorities objected very seriously. About the end of April or the beginning of May, when he got through with his driving operations, and had a crew of about 150 men in town, we all went to bed in a peaceful way one night, as we do in that country, and when we woke up in the morning we found a railway running through

our main street. It was there for some years. Under present conditions the board would 'have power to deal with it, but there is an instance where this mill-owner would have been glad to get that right for $5,000. As a matter of fact he got it for less than that because he simply built the spur during the night. Were any reasons given why the penalty was limited?
There were no reasons given.

Section agreed to.
On section 405-Failure to erect signboards at crossings.
The only change is that the word " railway " is added after the word " every " in the first line.

My hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) asks me whether I do not think there should be something more than the ordinary sign " Railway crossing." I am not sure whether the law provides what the sign shall be. I know the Canadian Pacific railway invariably put up two boards, one across the other. I think that is really more effective than any printing you might have on the boards. I do not know whether it is provided for by statute or not.
Why do you think it is better than the other?

If you simply have two boards, with nothing on them, I think they would arrest the attention of the average traveller more than if you had the words
" Stop! look! listen!" on a single board. Section agreed to.
On section 407-Safety and care of roadway, etc.
The only change is the addition of the word " wilfully" after the word " or " in the third line of subsection (d).
In case some one passing through left the gate open and the cattle got in and were killed, who -would be responsible for them?
The farmer.
Is he supposed to keep the gate locked?
That is covered in another clause.

If my hon. friend will go back to section 387 he will find it specifically stated that the company is not liable 
if somebody leaves the gate open. I think that is only fair. The railway company must provide suitable gates, and if they do not the Board will compel them to do so I know in many cases the gates are not what they should be. However, the farmer has his redress by coming before the Board and having an order issued to the company to install suitable gates. If a tramp comes along in the night and leaves the gate open I do not think the railway company should be held responsible for it. It seems to me that would be carrying the thing to extremes; it would be making the company an insurer against every man's negligence and almost against his criminality.
I think that is fair enough. A farmer could keep the gate locked.
Where land is being taken, that should be considered in fixing the compensation. It is a great inconvenience to the farmer to watch these gates.

That goes back to the question of compensation at the time the right of way is taken. There are a great many times that the poor farmer, in settling for the right of way, does not realize what it means to be compelled to drive his stock and operate his farm across a railway, but still the principle involved in settling compensation is that once settled that is an end to it.
On section 413-notification of accidents
The only change is the insertion of the word "railway" after the word "every" in the first line.

That runs all through the Bill, and the reason is that in the old Act the word "company" only meant a railway company by the definition. Now the word "company" means every company over which the Parliament of Canada has jurisdiction-electric light, power, telegraph or telephone company. Therefore, in these particular sections, it is necessary to insert the word "railway" in order to make it intelligible.

Section agreed to.
, On section 416-blackboard; notice of overdue trains:

The changes are these: The word "railway" is inserted after the word "any" in the first line; the words "or telephone" are inserted after the word "telegraph" in the second line, and the words "or telephone" are inserted in the last line of paragraph (a).

I do not think that is fair to a railway company under certain conditions. If any railway company, upon whose railway there is a telegraph or telephone line, does not put a blackboard up and give notice of the time at which trains will arrive, or as to whether they are late or not, it shall be liable. That would be all right in the case of a railway company that is operating its road by telephone or telegraph. That is becoming very prevalent. There are many railways that are being operated by telephone and I think on some portions of the big railway systems they are using the telephone almost exclusively, and, I believe, with very great benefit. But in eastern Canada practically all the telephone companies have instruments in the railway stations. I happen to have a little knowledge about telephone matters in New Brunswick. There was a time when our telephone instruments were put into the railway stations practically without any compensation, but an arrangement was made by which they pay a certain rental. I have known cases in which an independent telephone company feels that it is to its interest to have an instrument placed in the railway station. For the purposes of my argument, it does not make any difference whether they are put there at the expense of the company or put there for the benefit of the telephone company and its patrons; the telephone is there. But the telephone, in this case absolutely plays no part whatever in the operation of the railway. You are providing that a railway must do certain things if they happen to have a telephone in their office. The section ought to be so worded as to provide that the railway should do these things when the telephone is there and is used, instead of the telegraph, by the company for the purpose of operating trains. I do not know whether this has been brought to the minister's attention.
No, it has not.
All over the country you will find telephones in railway offices which are there purely for the accommodation of the public and play no part whatever in the operation of the railway.

They are installing the telephone to a great extent on the main lines, and this clause must be taken in connection with clause 304 dealing with blackboards at stations, overdue trains and further notice in English and French.
That is quite true.

I quite understand what the hon. gentleman means when he says that telephones are frequently placed in the stations, and we compel the companies to allow them to be placed there for the convenience of the people. The hon. gentleman thinks that possibly there might be an unfair advantage taken of the railway under this clause?
Yes, unless the telephone is owned or leased by the railway company for the purpose- of operating its trains.

There would not be
many branch railways in your country operating by telephone.

To a certain extent. My own town is a divisional point and trains are operated by telephone nearly 150 miles each way from the station. I happen to know one point on that line within two or three miles of town. It is a junction point, and they have telephonic communication between that junction point and the despatching office. When a conductor on that particular line reaches the junction he telephones in to the head office. As far as that particular line is concerned they aTe operating by telephone. That case would come under the provisions of this section. But that same office has -another telephone in it-a telephone of what is called the Farmers' line, and it has no relation whatever to the operation of the railway. I do not know that this is putting very much of a burden on the railway company, but I felt like pointing out the difficulty. I am sure that if the railways had noticed it there would have been some discussion.
I do not think it would operate to their disadvantage in our district. I am sure it is the proper thing to do in the more thickly settled portions of the country.
It means that the railway must at once put telephones into the offices.
It would only be objectionable to apply this provision where there was no station house, and we might limit it to places where there are station houses occupied by the company.

It is -all in the hands of the railway company because it is optional with them whether they -allow a telephone company to install a telephone in their station. In Peterborough they have

Then the public have
